newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan officials laying sea road to oil tanker bow.
newsitem.headline: Japan officials laying sea road to oil tanker bow.

text.p: Japanese maritime officials were on Saturday building a causeway across rough seas to reach the grounded bow of a ruptured oil tanker and drain off remaining oil as bad weather halted an earlier operation by ship, a Maritime Safety Agency (MSA) spokesman said.
"We're building a causeway with rocks to get to the tanker bow because bad weather has blocked drainage operations by ship," the maritime official said.
"The access road is almost completed, leaving around 200 metres from the coast to where the bow has run aground," he said.
Oil leaked from tanks in the bow of the Russian vessel has so far caused most of the pollution along a 500 km (325 mile) stretch of coast about 300 km (190 miles) west of Tokyo.

Sixty-three MSA boats were continuing a cleanup operation on Saturday of oil slicks still leaking from the sunken stern of the ageing 13,157-tonne Nakhodka and being driven by wind and tides towards land, the agency official said.
The agency had still not located the exact position of the stern of the 26-year-old vessel which held most of the 19,000-tonne (133,000-barrel) cargo of heavy oil, the spokesman said.
"We are collecting data right now. We'll only be able to analyse that once it's brought back to land... When that will be I'm not sure," he said.
The stern was thought to have sunk about 130 km (80 miles) off the coast of Shimane Prefecture shortly after the ship broke up in rough seas on January 2.

In a sad twist in the 16-day-old pollution crisis on the northern Japanese coast, the oil spill forced evacuation on Friday of 14 dolphins from the Echizen Matsushima Aquarium, only one mile (two km) from the bow of the tanker.
Seven of the dolphins, including a seven-month-old, were headed for Kobe on the day that it commemorated the second anniversary of an earthquake that devastated the city.

Six prefectures heavily dependent on fisheries and tourism, are already involved in a non-stop struggle to protect and clean shores dotted with shellfish farms, scenic beaches and marine bird sanctuaries.

Japan's Defence Academy reported on Friday that the spill would have minimal impact on deep-sea marine resources, such as crab, one of the local specialties, because little oil was dissolved by sea water.
The academy also reported the impact on oil-hit beaches would not be as bad as expected as the oil had not been absorbed deeply into the sand.
MSA officials were waiting for the second of two specialised oil slick cleanup vessels sent by Russia to arrive before the vessels could begin operations.
Officials said bad weather was impeding the progress of the 2.317-tonne Neftegas-5 and it was not sure when it would join the 1,120-tonne Lazurit which arrived yesterday.
Despite Moscow's decision to send three ships to help with the cleanup, Japan has lashed out at Russia for what it regards as a half-hearted response so far to the leaks.
The 31-man crew of the tanker, which was heading from China to Russia, was rescued. The captain is missing and presumed dead.
MSA officials said on Saturday agency boats had collected a total of 283 tonnes of oil from the sea, out of a current estimate of 5,000 tonnes leaked from the Nakhodka.
